tier2.text: Each sublingual gland makes saliva and sends it into the mouth through the lesser sublingual ducts, tubes through which a gland releases its contents. Each sublingual gland lies in the floor of the mouth beneath the tongue, in front of the submandibular gland. The sublingual glands are one of the three pairs of major salivary glands; the other two are the parotid and submandibular glands. Each sublingual gland contains mostly mucous cells, which secrete mucus, a thick, slippery substance that keeps tissues moist. The sublingual glands secrete the thickest saliva, with the least salivary amylase, which breaks down starch. The high mucus content of this saliva lubricates food for swallowing. Chemicals in food stimulate taste receptors on the tongue, which signal the brain stem to send back nerve impulses that stimulate salivation. The impulses that reach each sublingual gland travel through the facial nerve.
